rules: A shipped intent's acceptance criterion is amended in place, never silently rewritten: quote what it said, date the amendment, and name the record or commit that superseded it. The precedent is iss-2609052143457583; visible prose, not an HTML comment.

Where an Audit Notes verdict below an amended criterion predates the rewrite, say so in the amendment — the verdict is the stale artefact, not the criterion. A NOT_MET verdict beside an already-amended criterion otherwise reads as a live failure (iss-2609091757014163).

Never hand-edit prose inside an Audit Notes verdict. `abcd intent audit ingest` writes one hunk at the heading and touches nothing above it, which is what makes criteria structurally hard to amend silently; a verdict edited by hand has no such protection and no provenance (iss-2609100633302137). If a verdict's evidence must change, re-run the audit, or add a dated note beside it rather than rewriting it.

An exception that is itself a rule: never quote replaced text when the replacement was a privacy scrub. Naming what was removed puts the banned name back into a committed record; say what class of thing was removed and cite the record instead.

A closed spec that says a thing was declined while the tree does that thing is a record that reads false. Amend it, and name which question was actually answered — a later decision on a different question is not a reversal of the first.

Never use `git checkout -- <path>`, `git restore`, `git stash`, `git reset --hard`, or `git clean` to undo a scratch edit. They discard to HEAD, not to the working state, and this repository's branches routinely carry a whole session of unstaged work (iss-2609100620246542: 93 lines of src/app.ts destroyed this way, recovered only by luck from a stale dist source map).

To make a temporary edit and undo it — proving a test is not vacuous, probing behaviour — copy the file aside and copy it back: `cp <path> /tmp/x.bak` then `cp /tmp/x.bak <path>`. Force the restore (`cp -f`, or `command cp`) because an interactive `cp -i` alias will stall a background job mid-restore and leave the file half-changed.

After any restore, verify it rather than assuming it: `git diff --numstat -- <path>` against what you expected to be there, and grep for a marker of each distinct piece of work the file should contain.

The session's opening `git status` snapshot is a point in time, not the current state. Never reason about whether a file is clean from it — run `git status --short -- <path>` at the moment you need the answer.
Proving a test fails without its fix is required, not optional, but it is done by editing forward and back, never by reverting to HEAD.
